l: seven years of service (Jacob for Rachel), Genesis, Chapter 29
s: Jacob proposes to serve seven years for Rachel, and the years seem to him but a few days because of his love for her. When they are fulfilled, Laban gives him Leah instead, and Jacob must serve seven more years to receive Rachel as well.

Rachel, barren, demands children from Jacob and gives him her servant Bilhah, who bears Dan and Naphtali; Leah responds by giving Jacob her servant Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher. Leah then trades her son Reuben's mandrakes to Rachel for a night with Jacob and bears Issachar, Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah, before God remembers Rachel and she bears Joseph. Jacob then asks Laban to let him leave with his wives and children, but Laban urges him to stay and name his wages. Jacob proposes taking the speckled, spotted, and black animals as his hire, and Laban agrees and removes those animals to his sons, three days' journey away. Jacob uses peeled rods at the watering troughs so the stronger flocks bear streaked and spotted young, and he grows exceedingly rich.

Rachel, childless, envies Leah and demands children from Jacob, then gives him her servant Bilhah so she may have children through her. She names Bilhah's sons Dan and Naphtali, trades Leah mandrakes for a night with Jacob, and finally has her own womb opened by God, bearing Joseph.

Jacob becomes angry at Rachel's demand, lies with Bilhah, Zilpah, and Leah, and fathers Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Dinah, and Joseph. He then asks Laban to send him away, negotiates a hire of the speckled, spotted, and black animals, and through his rod method becomes exceedingly wealthy with large flocks, servants, camels, and donkeys.

Leah, having stopped bearing, gives her servant Zilpah to Jacob and names Gad and Asher. She hires Jacob for a night with her son Reuben's mandrakes, conceives Issachar and Zebulun, and bears a daughter, Dinah.

Laban asks Jacob to stay because he has divined that the LORD blessed him for Jacob's sake, and agrees to Jacob's proposed wages. He then has the streaked, spotted, and black animals removed and given to his sons, setting three days' journey between himself and Jacob.
Bilhah, Rachel's servant, is given to Jacob as a wife. She conceives and bears him two sons, who are named Dan and Naphtali.
Zilpah, Leah's servant, is given to Jacob as a wife by Leah. She bears him two sons, named Gad and Asher.
God is invoked by Jacob as the one who withholds the fruit of the womb, and is credited by the women for the births. He listens to Leah and she conceives, and he remembers Rachel and opens her womb.

l: flocks (Laban's and Jacob's livestock), Genesis, Chapter 30
s: The flocks increased from little to a multitude under Jacob's care. After the spotted and dark animals are removed, the flocks conceive in front of the peeled rods and produce streaked, speckled, and spotted young, with the stronger ones becoming Jacob's and the feebler Laban's.

Jacob takes fresh rods of poplar, almond, and plane tree and peels white streaks in them. He sets them in the watering troughs in front of the flocks, and the flocks that conceive before them produce streaked, speckled, and spotted young.

l: wages agreement (Jacob and Laban's hire), Genesis, Chapter 30
s: Jacob declines a set payment and proposes that his hire be every speckled, spotted, and black animal, with any other animal found with him counted as stolen. Laban agrees, and the terms lead to Jacob's great increase in flocks.

l: children (Rachel and Jacob's wives' children), Genesis, Chapter 30
s: Through Leah, Bilhah, Zilpah, and Rachel, Jacob has sons Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, and Joseph, plus a daughter, Dinah, along with Reuben, who is already Leah's son. Their names are given with explanations tied to the rivalry between Rachel and Leah.

Jacob hears Laban's sons complaining that he has taken their father's wealth and sees that Laban's attitude has cooled, and the LORD tells him to return to the land of his fathers. Jacob explains to Rachel and Leah how God has prospered him and how Laban has cheated him, and they agree to go. Jacob secretly flees with his family and livestock while Laban is shearing sheep, and Rachel steals her father's teraphim. Laban pursues Jacob for seven days to the mountain of Gilead, but God warns him in a dream not to speak to Jacob either good or bad. After Laban searches the tents without finding the teraphim, which Rachel is hiding under her in a camel's saddle, Jacob angrily recounts his twenty years of service, and the two men make a covenant with a heap of stones and a pillar as witness. Jacob offers a sacrifice and a meal, and Laban kisses and blesses his sons and daughters and returns home.

Jacob hears the complaints of Laban's sons, is told by the LORD to return home, and persuades Rachel and Leah to leave with him. He flees secretly with his family and livestock, and when Laban overtakes him he denies knowing about the stolen teraphim and angrily recounts his twenty years of faithful service. He sets up a pillar, makes a covenant with Laban, swears by the fear of Isaac, and offers a sacrifice.

Laban's face is no longer favorable toward Jacob, and he pursues the fleeing Jacob for seven days to Gilead with his relatives. Warned by God in a dream not to speak to Jacob either good or bad, he nonetheless accuses Jacob of deceit and of stealing his gods, searches the tents without finding them, and then proposes a covenant. He kisses and blesses his sons and daughters and returns to his place.

Rachel, with Leah, answers Jacob that they have no portion left in their father's house, are treated as foreigners, and that Jacob should do whatever God has said. She steals her father's teraphim, hides them in the camel's saddle, and sits on them, telling Laban she cannot rise because she is having her period, so he does not find them.

Leah, together with Rachel, is called by Jacob to the field and agrees to leave, saying their father has sold them and used up their money. Laban searches her tent for his gods but does not find them.

God tells Jacob to return to the land of his fathers and promises to be with him, and Jacob says God took Laban's livestock and gave it to him, and identifies himself as the God of Bethel. He warns Laban in a dream not to speak to Jacob either good or bad, and is invoked as witness and judge in the covenant, called the God of Abraham, the God of Nahor, and the fear of Isaac.

Rachel steals Laban's teraphim while he is shearing sheep. Laban accuses Jacob of stealing them, and Jacob, not knowing Rachel took them, says whoever has them shall not live. Rachel hides them in the camel's saddle and sits on them, so Laban's search of the tents does not find them.

Jacob tells Rachel and Leah that the flock bore speckled and streaked young according to the wages Laban named, and that God has taken Laban's livestock and given it to him. Jacob takes all his livestock, including what he gained in Paddan Aram, when he leaves, and says he bore the losses of torn animals during his years of service.

Gilead is the mountain toward which Jacob sets his face after crossing the River. Laban overtakes him there after seven days, and both camp in the mountain, where God warns Laban in a dream and where the covenant is made.

Jacob's relatives gather stones into a heap beside the pillar Jacob sets up, and they eat there. Laban calls it Jegar Sahadutha and Jacob calls it Galeed, and it is also named Mizpah. It stands as a witness that neither man will pass over it to harm the other.

l: covenant between Jacob and Laban, Genesis, Chapter 31
s: Laban proposes a covenant to serve as a witness between himself and Jacob. They agree that Jacob will not afflict Laban's daughters or take other wives, and that neither will pass over the heap and pillar to harm the other, with God as witness and judge. Jacob swears by the fear of Isaac and then offers a sacrifice and shares a meal.

l: Jacob's flight from Laban, Genesis, Chapter 31
s: After the LORD's command and the agreement of Rachel and Leah, Jacob secretly leaves with his wives, children, and livestock without telling Laban. Laban learns of it on the third day and overtakes him in Gilead after seven days. Laban accuses Jacob of stealing away his daughters and gods, the search turns up nothing, and the confrontation ends in a covenant and Laban's departure.

Jacob travels on and is met by angels of God, naming the place Mahanaim. He sends messengers to his brother Esau, who return saying Esau is coming with four hundred men, and Jacob, greatly afraid, divides his company into two, prays to God for deliverance, and prepares a large present of livestock to appease Esau. That night he sends his wives, servants, sons, and possessions across the ford of the Jabbok and is left alone, wrestling with a man until daybreak. The man strains Jacob's thigh, renames him Israel, and blesses him; Jacob names the place Peniel, saying he has seen God face to face, and limps away at sunrise, which is given as the reason the children of Israel do not eat the sinew of the hip.

Jacob is met by angels, sends messengers to Esau, and becomes greatly afraid on learning Esau approaches with four hundred men. He divides his people into two companies, prays to God, sends a present ahead, and crosses his family over the Jabbok before wrestling alone with a man until daybreak. He refuses to let the man go without a blessing, is renamed Israel, names the place Peniel, and limps away with a strained thigh.

Esau, Jacob's brother, lives in the land of Seir, the field of Edom, and receives Jacob's messengers calling him 'my lord.' The messengers report he is coming to meet Jacob with four hundred men, which terrifies Jacob. Jacob plans to appease him with a present and hopes he will accept him.

God is addressed by Jacob as the God of Abraham and Isaac, who told him to return to his country and promised to do him good and make his offspring as the sand of the sea. His angels meet Jacob, who calls them God's army. Jacob says after the wrestling that he has seen God face to face and his life was preserved.

l: present (Jacob's present for Esau), Genesis, Chapter 32
s: Jacob takes from his possessions a present for Esau: goats, ewes, rams, milk camels with colts, cows, bulls, donkeys, and foals. He gives it to his servants in separate herds with spaces between them, instructing them to tell Esau the animals are Jacob's gift and that Jacob is behind them. Jacob intends it to appease Esau so that he might accept him, and it passes over before him.

A man wrestles Jacob at the Jabbok until daybreak and, seeing he does not prevail, touches the hollow of Jacob's thigh and strains it. He asks Jacob's name, renames him Israel because he has fought with God and men and prevailed, and blesses him. He declines to give his own name, asking why Jacob asks.

After crossing his family over the ford of the Jabbok, Jacob is left alone and wrestles with a man until the breaking of day. The man strains Jacob's thigh, and Jacob will not let go without a blessing, receiving the name Israel. The place is named Peniel, Jacob limps afterward, and the event is given as the reason the children of Israel do not eat the sinew of the hip.

Jacob sees Esau approaching with four hundred men and arranges his family in order, with the servants first, Leah next, and Rachel and Joseph last. He bows seven times as he approaches, and Esau runs to embrace him, and the two brothers weep. Jacob introduces his children, and each group bows before Esau. Jacob urges Esau to accept his gift, and Esau finally takes it. Esau returns toward Seir, while Jacob goes to Succoth, then to Shechem in Canaan, where he buys a parcel of land from the children of Hamor for one hundred pieces of money and erects an altar called El Elohe Israel.

Jacob arranges his family in order and goes ahead of them, bowing to the ground seven times before Esau. He urges Esau to accept his gift, saying he has seen Esau's face as one sees the face of God, and he declines Esau's offer of an escort, citing the tender children and the flocks. He then travels to Succoth, builds a house and shelters, comes in peace to Shechem, buys the ground where he pitched his tent, and erects the altar El Elohe Israel.

Esau comes with four hundred men, runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, falls on his neck, kisses him, and weeps. He asks about the women and children and about the company he met, says he has enough, and accepts the gift only after Jacob urges him. He offers to travel ahead and to leave some of his people with Jacob, and when Jacob declines, he returns that day toward Seir.

Jacob divides the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two servants, with the servants' children in front, Leah's next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear. Jacob tells Esau they are the children God has graciously given him, and each group comes near and bows before Esau. Jacob later cites their tenderness as the reason for traveling slowly.

l: present (Jacob's present for Esau), Genesis, Chapter 33
s: Jacob explains that the company Esau met was sent to find favor in his sight. Esau first says he has enough and refuses it, but Jacob insists, saying God has dealt graciously with him and that he has enough, and Esau takes it.

l: reconciliation of Jacob and Esau, Genesis, Chapter 33
s: Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces and kisses him, and the two weep, showing a peaceful meeting where Jacob had approached with deference. Esau accepts the gift and offers to accompany Jacob, but Jacob asks to follow at his own pace toward Seir. The brothers then part, with Esau returning to Seir and Jacob traveling to Succoth.

Dinah, Jacob's daughter, goes out to see the women of the land, and Shechem, son of the Hivite prince Hamor, takes her, lies with her, and humbles her, then asks his father to get her as a wife. Hamor and Shechem propose intermarriage and shared land to Jacob and his sons, and Shechem offers any dowry. Jacob's sons answer deceitfully, demanding that every male of the city be circumcised, and the men of the city agree after Hamor and Shechem persuade them at the gate. On the third day, while the men are sore, Simeon and Levi kill all the males, including Hamor and Shechem, and take Dinah out of Shechem's house. The other sons plunder the city and take its flocks, wealth, women, and children, and Jacob rebukes Simeon and Levi for making him odious among the inhabitants, while they reply by asking whether their sister should be treated like a prostitute.

Dinah, daughter of Leah and Jacob, goes out to see the daughters of the land and is taken, lain with, and humbled by Shechem. She is later taken out of Shechem's house by her brothers Simeon and Levi after the killing of the city's males.

Jacob hears that Dinah has been defiled and holds his peace until his sons come in from the field. After Simeon and Levi's attack he rebukes them for making him odious among the Canaanites and Perizzites, fearing that, being few in number, he and his house will be destroyed.

Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite and prince of the land, takes and lies with Dinah, then loves her, speaks kindly to her, and asks his father to get her as a wife. He offers any dowry to her father and brothers, is quick to be circumcised, and is killed by the sword with his father.

Hamor, father of Shechem, goes out to Jacob and proposes intermarriage, shared land, and trade. He accepts the circumcision condition and persuades the men at the city gate, arguing that Jacob's livestock and possessions would become theirs, and is later killed by Simeon and Levi.

Jacob's sons come in from the field grieved and very angry that folly was done in Israel. They answer Shechem and Hamor with deceit, demanding circumcision, and afterward plunder the city, taking its animals, wealth, women, and little ones.

Simeon, a brother of Dinah, takes his sword with Levi, comes upon the unsuspecting city on the third day, and kills all the males, including Hamor and Shechem. Jacob rebukes him along with Levi for the consequences.

Levi, a brother of Dinah, takes his sword with Simeon and kills all the males of the city, including Hamor and Shechem. With Simeon he is rebuked by Jacob and answers by asking whether their sister should be treated as a prostitute.

l: men of Shechem's city, Genesis, Chapter 34
s: The men who went out of the city gate listen to Hamor and Shechem and every male is circumcised, persuaded by the prospect of peace, intermarriage, and gaining the newcomers' livestock and possessions. On the third day, while sore, all the males are killed by Simeon and Levi.

The city, whose gate is the site of Hamor and Shechem's address to its men, is come upon unsuspecting on the third day after the circumcision. It is plundered of its flocks, herds, donkeys, wealth, and houses' contents, and its wives and little ones are taken captive.

Jacob's sons set circumcision of every male as the condition for giving and taking daughters and becoming one people, calling an uncircumcised husband a reproach. The city's males all undergo it, and on the third day, while they are sore, they are killed.

Shechem's taking and lying with Dinah is called defiling her, and it provokes grief and anger in Jacob's sons as folly in Israel, a thing that ought not to be done. It is given as the reason for their deceitful answer and for the plunder, and the sons cite it in their final reply to Jacob.

l: massacre and plunder of the city, Genesis, Chapter 34
s: Simeon and Levi kill all the males of the city with swords, including Hamor and Shechem, and remove Dinah from Shechem's house. Jacob's sons then plunder the city's livestock, wealth, and houses and take the women and little ones captive, which Jacob fears will bring the inhabitants against him.

God tells Jacob to go to Bethel and build an altar, so Jacob has his household give up their foreign gods and rings, which he hides under the oak by Shechem. They travel safely to Bethel, where Jacob builds an altar, Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, dies, and God appears again, renaming Jacob Israel and repeating the promise of land and descendants. Leaving Bethel, Rachel dies in hard labor near Ephrath after giving birth to Benjamin, and Jacob sets up a pillar on her grave. Reuben lies with Bilhah, and the twelve sons of Jacob are listed. Jacob then reaches his father Isaac at Mamre (Hebron), where Isaac dies at one hundred eighty and is buried by Esau and Jacob.

Jacob obeys God's command to go to Bethel, has his household put away their foreign gods and hides them under the oak by Shechem, and builds an altar at Bethel. God renames him Israel and repeats the promise of nation, kings and land; Jacob sets up a stone pillar, pours a drink offering and oil on it, and later sets a pillar on Rachel's grave. He names Rachel's newborn son Benjamin, hears of Reuben's act with Bilhah, and returns to his father Isaac at Mamre, helping Esau bury him.

God commands Jacob to go up to Bethel and build an altar, and a terror from God keeps the surrounding cities from pursuing Jacob's sons. God appears again to Jacob, blesses him, changes his name to Israel, identifies himself as God Almighty, and promises a nation, a company of nations, kings, and the land given to Abraham and Isaac.

Bethel, also called Luz, is in the land of Canaan, and Jacob builds an altar there and calls the place El Beth El because God was revealed to him there when he fled from his brother. God speaks with Jacob there again, and Jacob sets up a stone pillar and names the place Bethel. Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, is buried below it under the oak called Allon Bacuth.
Isaac is at Mamre, Kiriath Arba (Hebron), when Jacob comes to him. He lives one hundred eighty years, dies, is gathered to his people old and full of days, and is buried by his sons Esau and Jacob.

Rachel goes into hard labor on the way from Bethel before reaching Ephrath, and the midwife tells her she will have another son. She dies as her soul departs, after naming the child Benoni, and is buried on the way to Ephrath (Bethlehem), where Jacob sets a pillar on her grave that remains to this day. She is listed as the mother of Joseph and Benjamin.

Benjamin is born to Rachel during her hard labor on the way to Ephrath. Rachel names him Benoni as she dies, but his father names him Benjamin. He is listed among the twelve sons of Jacob as a son of Rachel with Joseph.
Reuben goes and lies with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel hears of it. He is listed as Jacob's firstborn and a son of Leah.

Isaac dies at the age of one hundred eighty after Jacob has come to him at Mamre (Hebron). He gives up the spirit and is gathered to his people, old and full of days, and his sons Esau and Jacob bury him.

l: Rachel's childbirth and death, Genesis, Chapter 35
s: On the journey from Bethel, some distance short of Ephrath, Rachel goes into hard labor, and the midwife reassures her that she will have another son. She dies as she gives birth, naming the boy Benoni while Jacob names him Benjamin. She is buried on the way to Ephrath (Bethlehem), and Jacob marks her grave with a pillar.

Genesis 36 records the generations of Esau, also called Edom. Esau took wives Adah, Oholibamah, and Basemath, who bore him sons in Canaan, and he then moved with his household and livestock to the hill country of Seir, away from his brother Jacob, because their possessions were too great for them to live together. The chapter lists Esau's descendants and the chiefs from Eliphaz, Reuel, and Oholibamah, including Amalek born to Timna, concubine of Eliphaz. It also lists the sons and chiefs of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land, including Anah who found the hot springs. Finally it names the eight kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel, and closes with a list of the chiefs of Edom according to their habitations.

Esau took wives Adah, Oholibamah, and Basemath, who bore Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah in Canaan. He gathered his household and livestock and moved to the hill country of Seir, away from Jacob, because their substance was too great to dwell together. He is identified as Edom and as the father of the Edomites.

Edom is identified as another name for Esau, who lived in the hill country of Seir. The land of Edom is where the chiefs of Eliphaz, Reuel, and the Horites are said to have come from, and where kings reigned before any king reigned over Israel.

Esau settled in the hill country of Seir after leaving Canaan and his brother Jacob. It is described as the land of the Horites, the children of Seir, who were its inhabitants, and Esau is called the father of the Edomites there.

The Horites are the sons of Seir, inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan, whose children and chiefs are listed. Their chiefs are named in the land of Seir and in the land of Edom, and Anah is noted for finding the hot springs in the wilderness while feeding his father Zibeon's donkeys.

Esau is named as the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir. Their descent is traced through Eliphaz, Reuel, and Oholibamah's sons, with lists of chiefs ending with chiefs according to their habitations in the land of their possession.

Eight kings reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel: Bela son of Beor, Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah, Husham of the Temanites, Hadad son of Bedad, Samlah of Masrekah, Shaul of Rehoboth by the river, Baal Hanan son of Achbor, and Hadar. Each reigned in place of the one who died; Hadad is noted as striking Midian in the field of Moab, and Hadar's wife was Mehetabel.

Joseph, seventeen and his father Israel's (Jacob's) favorite, is given a tunic of many colors and tells his brothers two dreams in which they and his parents bow to him, deepening their hatred. Jacob sends him to check on his brothers and the flock; he finds them at Dothan, where they plot to kill him. Reuben persuades them to throw him into an empty pit instead, and Judah then proposes selling him to a passing Ishmaelite caravan; Midianite merchants draw him out and sell him for twenty pieces of silver, taking him to Egypt. The brothers dip his tunic in goat's blood and show it to Jacob, who concludes an animal devoured Joseph and mourns inconsolably. The Midianites sell Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh's captain of the guard.

Joseph, seventeen years old, brings an evil report of his brothers to their father, is loved most by Israel, and tells two dreams of his family bowing to him. Sent by his father to find his brothers, he is found at Dothan, stripped of his tunic, thrown into a pit, and sold for twenty pieces of silver into Egypt, where he is sold to Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard.

Jacob, also called Israel, lives in Canaan and loves Joseph more than his other sons, making him a tunic of many colors. He rebukes Joseph's second dream but keeps it in mind, sends Joseph to check on his brothers, and is deceived by the bloodied tunic into believing Joseph was devoured. He tears his clothes, wears sackcloth, mourns many days, and refuses comfort, saying he will go down to Sheol mourning.

The brothers hate Joseph for their father's favoritism and for his dreams, and envy him. At Dothan they conspire to kill him, strip his tunic, throw him in a pit, and sell him to traders, then dip the tunic in goat's blood and deceive Jacob with it.

Reuben hears the plot to kill Joseph and objects, urging them to shed no blood and to throw him into the pit instead, intending to restore him to his father. When he returns and finds the pit empty, he tears his clothes and says to his brothers, "The child is no more; and I, where will I go?"

Judah asks what profit there is in killing their brother and concealing his blood. He proposes selling Joseph to the Ishmaelites, since Joseph is their brother and flesh, and his brothers listen to him.
A caravan of Ishmaelites comes from Gilead with camels bearing spices, balm, and myrrh, going down to Egypt. Joseph is sold to them for twenty pieces of silver.

Midianite merchants pass by, draw Joseph up out of the pit, and sell him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, bringing him into Egypt. They are also said to have sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh.

Egypt is the destination of the caravan carrying spices, balm, and myrrh, and of Joseph, who is brought there by the merchants. There he is sold to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.

l: tunic of many colors, Genesis, Chapter 37
s: Israel makes the tunic of many colors for Joseph, which marks his favored status and fuels his brothers' hatred. The brothers strip it from him at Dothan, dip it in goat's blood, and bring it to Jacob as false evidence that Joseph was killed, and Jacob recognizes it.

Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves bow to his sheaf, and then that the sun, moon, and eleven stars bow to him. His brothers hate him all the more and his father rebukes him, though Jacob keeps the saying in mind; the brothers later mock him as "this dreamer" and say they will see what becomes of his dreams.

The pit in the wilderness is empty, with no water, and is where the brothers throw Joseph after stripping him. Reuben intends it to keep Joseph alive, and the merchants later draw Joseph out of it, so Reuben finds it empty on his return.

On Judah's proposal, Joseph is sold for twenty pieces of silver to the Ishmaelites by passing Midianite merchants, who lift him out of the pit and bring him to Egypt. The brothers conceal the sale with a goat's-blood-stained tunic, and Joseph is ultimately sold to Potiphar.

Judah leaves his brothers, settles near Hirah the Adullamite, marries Shua's daughter, and has three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Judah gives Er a wife, Tamar, but the LORD kills Er for wickedness, and then kills Onan for refusing to give offspring to his brother through Tamar. Judah tells Tamar to wait as a widow in her father's house until Shelah is grown, but does not give her to him. Tamar veils herself at the gate of Enaim, Judah takes her for a prostitute and gives her his signet, cord, and staff as a pledge, and she conceives. When Tamar is accused of prostitution and sentenced to burning, she produces the pledge items, Judah acknowledges she is more righteous than he, and she bears twins, Perez and Zerah.

Judah settles near Hirah the Adullamite, marries Shua's daughter, and fathers Er, Onan, and Shelah. After his sons Er and Onan die, he sends Tamar away to wait for Shelah but does not give her to him, and later unknowingly sleeps with her, leaving his signet, cord, and staff as a pledge. When she shows the pledge, he acknowledges she is more righteous than he, and he does not know her again.

Tamar is given as wife to Er, is widowed, and is told by Judah to remain a widow in her father's house until Shelah is grown. Seeing that Shelah is grown and she was not given to him, she veils herself at Enaim, conceives by Judah, and secures his signet, cord, and staff. Condemned to burning, she proves the father with the pledge, is declared more righteous than Judah, and bears twins, Perez and Zerah.
Er is Judah's firstborn, and Judah takes Tamar as his wife. He is wicked in the LORD's sight, and the LORD kills him.

Onan is Judah's second son, born to Shua's daughter, and is told to go in to his brother's wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Knowing the offspring wouldn't be his, he spills his semen on the ground, which is evil in the LORD's sight, and the LORD kills him.
Shelah is Judah's third son, born at Chezib. Judah withholds him from Tamar, fearing he too will die like his brothers, even after he is grown, and Judah later admits he did not give her to Shelah.
Perez is one of Tamar's twin sons by Judah. He comes out second after his brother's hand appears, drawing back in a way that makes the midwife say he has made a breach, hence his name.
Zerah is Tamar's other twin son by Judah. His hand comes out first and the midwife ties a scarlet thread on it, but he is born after Perez.
Enaim is a place on the way to Timnah with a gate where Tamar sits veiled and meets Judah. When Judah's friend asks the men there about a prostitute, they say none has been there.

l: pledge (Judah's signet, cord and staff), Genesis, Chapter 38
s: Judah gives his signet, cord, and staff to the veiled Tamar as a pledge until he sends a young goat. His friend cannot find her to redeem it, and Judah lets her keep it. Tamar later sends the items to him as proof of the father of her child, and Judah acknowledges them.

l: Levirate duty (duty of a husband's brother), Genesis, Chapter 38
s: Judah commands Onan to go in to Er's widow Tamar and perform the duty of a husband's brother to raise up offspring for Er. Onan evades it and is killed. Judah then withholds Shelah from fulfilling it, which he later admits was wrong.

Joseph is brought down to Egypt and bought by Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, from the Ishmaelites. Because the LORD is with Joseph, he prospers and is made overseer over Potiphar's entire house, and the LORD blesses Potiphar's household for his sake. Potiphar's wife repeatedly asks Joseph to lie with her; he refuses, citing his master's trust and sin against God, and when she catches his garment he flees, leaving it in her hand. She uses the garment to accuse Joseph falsely before the men of her house and then Potiphar, who in wrath puts Joseph into the prison where the king's prisoners are bound. There the LORD is again with Joseph, giving him favor with the keeper of the prison, who puts all the prisoners under Joseph's charge and lets him run everything because the LORD makes his work prosper.

Joseph is brought to Egypt, sold to Potiphar, and prospers as overseer of his household because the LORD is with him. He refuses the advances of his master's wife, saying it would be great wickedness and sin against God, and flees, leaving his garment behind. Falsely accused, he is imprisoned, but again gains favor and is put in charge of all the prisoners.

Potiphar, an Egyptian officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, buys Joseph from the Ishmaelites and sees that the LORD is with him. He makes Joseph overseer of his house and entrusts everything to him except his own food. After hearing his wife's accusation, his wrath is kindled and he puts Joseph into the king's prison.

Potiphar's wife sets her eyes on Joseph and asks him to lie with her, speaking to him day by day. When he flees and leaves his garment in her hand, she calls the men of her house and then tells her husband that the Hebrew servant came in to mock her. She keeps the garment beside her until Potiphar comes home.

The LORD is with Joseph in Potiphar's house, making all he does prosper and blessing Potiphar's house and field for Joseph's sake. In the prison the LORD again is with Joseph, shows him kindness, gives him favor with the keeper, and makes what he does prosper.

The prison is the place where the king's prisoners are bound, and Joseph is put there in custody by his master. There Joseph is given charge of all the prisoners and is responsible for whatever they do.

l: keeper of the prison, Genesis, Chapter 39
s: The keeper of the prison, favorably disposed to Joseph through the LORD's doing, commits all the prisoners to Joseph's hand. He does not look after anything under Joseph's care because the LORD is with Joseph and makes his work prosper.

Joseph leaves his garment in the hand of Potiphar's wife when she catches him and he runs outside. She keeps it beside her and uses it as supposed evidence in her account to the men of her house and to Potiphar.

l: false accusation of attempted assault, Genesis, Chapter 39
s: After Joseph flees, Potiphar's wife claims that the Hebrew servant came in to lie with her and to mock her, and that he left his garment when she cried out. Hearing this, Potiphar becomes wrathful and imprisons Joseph, though the text shows Joseph had refused her.

Pharaoh, angry at his chief cup bearer and chief baker, puts them in the prison in the captain of the guard's house, where Joseph is bound and is assigned to care for them. After both men dream in one night, Joseph sees they are sad and, saying interpretations belong to God, asks them to tell him their dreams. He interprets the cup bearer's vine dream to mean restoration to office in three days and asks to be remembered to Pharaoh, then interprets the baker's dream of birds eating bread from baskets to mean he will be hanged in three days. On Pharaoh's birthday both outcomes happen as Joseph said, but the restored cup bearer forgets Joseph.

Joseph, bound in the prison, is assigned to care for Pharaoh's two officers and notices they are sad. He says interpretations belong to God, interprets both dreams, and asks the cup bearer to remember him and mention him to Pharaoh, saying he was stolen from the land of the Hebrews and has done nothing to deserve the dungeon. His interpretations prove true, but the cup bearer forgets him.

Pharaoh, called king of Egypt, becomes angry with his chief cup bearer and chief baker and puts them in custody. On his birthday he holds a feast for his servants, restores the cup bearer to his position and hangs the baker.

The chief cup bearer offends Pharaoh and is imprisoned, then dreams of a vine with three branches and tells it to Joseph. Joseph says he will be restored within three days, which happens on Pharaoh's birthday when he again gives the cup into Pharaoh's hand. He does not remember Joseph but forgets him.

The chief baker offends Pharaoh and is imprisoned, and after seeing that the cup bearer's interpretation was good, tells Joseph his dream of three baskets of white bread with birds eating from the top one. Joseph says he will be hanged within three days, and Pharaoh hangs him on his birthday as interpreted.

The prison is in the house of the captain of the guard and is the place where Joseph is bound. Pharaoh's cup bearer and baker are held there, and Joseph says he was put in its dungeon though he had done nothing wrong.

In the dream, a vine with three branches buds, blossoms and produces ripe grapes, which the cup bearer presses into Pharaoh's cup and gives into Pharaoh's hand. Joseph interprets the three branches as three days, after which Pharaoh will restore him to his office.

Joseph asks whether interpretations belong to God before hearing the dreams, then gives the cup bearer a favorable interpretation and the baker an unfavorable one. Both are fulfilled on the third day, as the text states when it says the baker was hanged as Joseph had interpreted.

Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cattle devoured by seven thin cattle and of seven healthy heads of grain swallowed by seven blasted ones, and none of Egypt's magicians and wise men can interpret them. The chief cup bearer recalls Joseph, who is brought from the dungeon and tells Pharaoh that the dream is one dream from God, foretelling seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. Joseph advises Pharaoh to appoint a discreet and wise man and overseers to collect a fifth of the produce and store grain in the cities. Pharaoh sets Joseph over all Egypt, gives him his signet ring, robes, a gold chain, the name Zaphenath-Paneah, and Asenath as a wife. Joseph stores grain in vast quantities during the plenty and has two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. When the famine comes, Egypt has bread, and Joseph sells grain to the Egyptians and to people from all countries.

Pharaoh dreams twice, is troubled, and finds that no magician or wise man can interpret the dreams. He summons Joseph, recounts the dreams, and accepts Joseph's interpretation and advice, then sets Joseph over all the land of Egypt, giving him his signet ring, fine linen robes, a gold chain, a new name, and Asenath as wife. During the famine he tells the Egyptians to go to Joseph and do what he says.

Joseph is brought hastily from the dungeon, shaves, changes his clothing, and appears before Pharaoh. He says the interpretation is not in him but that God will give Pharaoh an answer, explains the dreams as seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and advises storing grain. Pharaoh sets him over Egypt at age thirty; he gathers grain, fathers Manasseh and Ephraim, and sells grain to Egyptians and to all countries during the famine.

According to Joseph, God has declared to Pharaoh through the dream what he is about to do, and the dream was doubled because the thing is established by God and will shortly come to pass. Pharaoh recognizes Joseph as a man in whom is the Spirit of God, and Joseph credits God with making him forget his toil and with making him fruitful in the land of his affliction.

Egypt is the land where Pharaoh's magicians and wise men fail to interpret the dreams, and Joseph is set over all of it. It produces abundantly for seven years, with food stored in its cities, and then suffers famine along with all lands, yet has bread. Egyptians cry to Pharaoh for bread, are sent to Joseph, and buy grain, and people from all countries come to Egypt to buy.

l: Pharaoh's dream of the cattle, Genesis, Chapter 41
s: In this dream Pharaoh stands by the river and sees seven sleek, fat cattle come up and feed in the marsh grass, followed by seven ugly, thin cattle that eat them up and remain as ugly as before. Joseph explains that the seven good cattle are seven years of plenty and the seven thin cattle are seven years of famine.

l: Pharaoh's dream of the grain, Genesis, Chapter 41
s: In his second dream Pharaoh sees seven healthy, good heads of grain on one stalk swallowed by seven thin heads blasted with the east wind. Joseph says it carries the same meaning as the cattle dream: the good heads are seven years of plenty and the blasted ones seven years of famine, and the dream is one.

l: seven years of plenty, Genesis, Chapter 41
s: Joseph foretells seven years of great plenty throughout Egypt, represented by the good cattle and heads of grain. They come as foretold, and the earth produces abundantly. During them Joseph gathers food, and his two sons are born before the famine. The years then come to an end.

Joseph interprets the thin cattle and blasted grain as seven years of famine that will follow the plenty, make the plenty forgotten, and consume the land. The famine begins just as Joseph said and is severe over all the earth. Egypt alone has bread, and Joseph opens the storehouses to sell grain.

Joseph advises taking a fifth of the produce in the plentiful years and storing grain under Pharaoh's hand in the cities so the land will not perish in the famine. He stores food in each city from the surrounding fields, laying up grain like the sand of the sea until he stops counting. In the famine he opens the storehouses and sells grain to the Egyptians and to people from all countries.

Jacob sends ten of his sons down to Egypt to buy grain during the famine, keeping Benjamin at home for fear of harm. Joseph, the governor, recognizes his brothers, who do not recognize him, and accuses them of being spies. He holds them in custody for three days, then keeps Simeon bound as a hostage and demands that they bring their youngest brother to prove their honesty. The brothers acknowledge guilt over their treatment of Joseph, and Joseph secretly weeps and returns each man's money to his sack. Back in Canaan, they tell Jacob everything and find the money in their sacks, and Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go despite Reuben's pledge.

Jacob tells his sons to go to Egypt to buy grain so that they may live, but he does not send Benjamin, fearing harm to him. When his sons return, he laments that he has been bereaved of Joseph and Simeon and refuses to let Benjamin go down, saying that harm to him would bring his gray hairs down to Sheol with sorrow.

Joseph, governor over the land and seller of grain, recognizes his brothers and acts like a stranger, speaking roughly and accusing them of being spies as he remembers his dreams about them. He imprisons them for three days, keeps Simeon bound, and weeps privately after overhearing their remorse. He orders their bags filled with grain and their money restored to their sacks.

The ten brothers go down to Egypt, bow to Joseph with faces to the earth, and do not recognize him. They insist they are honest men, say they are twelve brothers, and admit among themselves they are guilty concerning Joseph. On the way home they find money in a sack and tremble, then report to Jacob and are afraid when all the money bundles are found.

Benjamin, Joseph's brother, is kept home by Jacob for fear of harm. Joseph demands that he be brought to Egypt as proof of the brothers' honesty, and Jacob refuses to let him go, calling him the only one left of his mother's sons.
Simeon is taken from among the brothers by Joseph and bound before their eyes, to remain in Egypt as a hostage until the youngest brother is brought. Jacob later laments that Simeon is no more.
Egypt is where grain is available during the famine, and Jacob sends his sons there to buy it. Joseph governs the land and sells to all its people.
Canaan is the land where the famine afflicts Jacob's family and from which the brothers travel to buy food. Jacob and Benjamin remain there, and the brothers return to report what happened.
Grain is bought in Egypt because of the famine, so that Jacob's family may live and not die. Joseph has the brothers' bags filled with it and sends it home for the famine of their houses.

The brothers' payment for grain is secretly restored by Joseph's command into each man's sack. One brother discovers his at the lodging place, and the rest find their bundles of money when they empty their sacks at home, leaving them frightened and asking what God has done to them.

Joseph accuses the brothers of being spies who have come to see the nakedness of the land, and repeats it when they deny it. He sets a test: one brother stays bound while the rest bring back the youngest, and he says this will verify their words. The brothers deny the charge, and Jacob is told of it on their return.

The famine in the land forces Israel to tell his sons to return to Egypt for food, and Judah pledges himself as collateral for Benjamin's safety so that their father will let the boy go. Israel agrees, sending a present, double money, and the money returned in the sacks, and the brothers take Benjamin down and stand before Joseph. Joseph has his steward bring them to his house for a noon meal, which frightens the brothers, who fear they will be seized over the returned money; the steward reassures them and brings Simeon out. When Joseph sees Benjamin he is overcome, weeps privately, then composes himself and serves the meal, giving Benjamin a portion five times larger than the others'.

Joseph sees Benjamin with the brothers and orders his steward to bring them to his house for a noon meal. He asks after their father, is moved to tears at the sight of Benjamin and weeps in his room, then washes his face, controls himself, and has the meal served. He seats the brothers by age and sends Benjamin a portion five times larger than the others'.

Israel, the father, tells his sons to buy more food, then reproaches them for telling the man about another brother. He yields to Judah's pledge and agrees to send Benjamin, instructing them to take a present, double money, and the returned money, and praying that God Almighty give them mercy. He resigns himself with the words, "If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved."

Judah reminds his father that the man said they would not see his face unless their brother came with them. He urges Israel to send the boy so that all may live, and offers himself as collateral, promising to bear the blame forever if he does not bring Benjamin back. His appeal persuades Israel.

Benjamin is sent down to Egypt with his brothers after Judah pledges to answer for him. Joseph sees him, calls him his brother, his mother's son, and blesses him, and is moved to tears. At the meal he is given a portion five times as large as any of his brothers'.

The brothers defend themselves to their father by saying they only answered the man's questions, then go down to Egypt with the present, double money, and Benjamin. Brought to Joseph's house, they fear arrest and enslavement over the returned money and explain themselves to the steward, who reassures them and brings Simeon out. They bow before Joseph, are seated by birthright and age, marvel at it, and drink and are merry with him.

The famine is severe in the land. It drives the story: the grain brought from Egypt is eaten up, and their father sends the sons back to buy more food. Judah argues that going is necessary so that they and their little ones may live and not die.

l: money returned in the sacks, Genesis, Chapter 43
s: The money found in the sacks on the first trip makes Israel suspect an oversight, so he tells his sons to bring it back along with double money. On arrival it makes the brothers fear that Joseph will seek occasion against them and seize them as slaves. They explain it to the steward, who says their God gave them treasure in their sacks and that he received their money.

Israel directs his sons to bring a present of choice fruits of the land: a little balm, honey, spices, myrrh, nuts, and almonds. The brothers prepare it for Joseph's arrival at noon and, when he comes home, bring it into the house and bow to the earth before him.

Joseph has his steward fill the men's sacks with food, return their money, and hide his silver cup in the youngest brother's sack. After the men leave, the steward overtakes them and accuses them of theft; they protest and pledge that whoever has the cup will die and the rest will become slaves. The cup is found in Benjamin's sack, and the brothers tear their clothes and return to Joseph's house. Joseph says only the one with the cup will be his slave, and the others may go in peace. Judah then pleads at length, recounting their father's love for the youngest son and fear of losing him, and offers to stay as Joseph's slave in the boy's place.

Joseph ordered his steward to fill the men's sacks, return their money, and put his silver cup in the youngest's sack, then sent the steward after them to accuse them of theft. When the cup was found, he said the one holding it would be his slave and the others could go in peace to their father, and he claimed that a man like him can do divination.

Judah spoke for the brothers before Joseph, saying God had found out their iniquity and offering that all of them be slaves. He then made a long plea recounting their father's love for the boy and fear of losing him, and offered to stay as Joseph's slave instead of the boy, because he had become collateral for him to their father.

Benjamin, the youngest brother, had Joseph's silver cup placed in his sack and it was found there. Joseph declared that he would be made a slave. Judah's speech describes him as the little child of his father's old age, the only one left of his mother, and the one his father loves.

Jacob, referred to as the brothers' father and as an old man, is described through Judah's account. He told his sons to go buy more food, and said he had lost one son, who he assumed was torn in pieces, and that losing the other would bring his gray hairs down to Sheol with sorrow. His life is said to be bound up in the boy's life.

The brothers were sent away with food, but were overtaken by the steward and accused of repaying good with evil. They rashly pledged that whoever had the cup would die and the rest become slaves, searched their sacks, and found the cup in Benjamin's. They tore their clothes, returned to the city, and fell on the ground before Joseph.

Joseph's silver cup was secretly put in the mouth of the youngest brother's sack. The steward said Joseph drinks from it and uses it to divine, and it was found in Benjamin's sack, which brought the accusation of theft against the brothers.

Joseph, unable to restrain himself, clears the room and reveals his identity to his brothers, weeping so loudly that the Egyptians and Pharaoh's house hear. He tells them not to be grieved, because God sent him ahead to preserve life during the five remaining years of famine, and he instructs them to bring their father to live near him in Goshen. After Joseph embraces and kisses his brothers, Pharaoh approves and orders them to fetch their father and households with wagons, promising the good of Egypt. Joseph sends them off with wagons, provisions, clothing, and extra gifts for Benjamin and for his father. In Canaan the brothers tell Jacob that Joseph is alive and ruling Egypt; he first disbelieves, but the sight of the wagons revives him and he resolves to go see Joseph before he dies.

Joseph clears the room, weeps aloud, and reveals himself to his brothers, telling them that God sent him ahead to preserve life and made him father to Pharaoh, lord of Pharaoh's house, and ruler of Egypt. He directs them to bring Jacob and their households to Goshen, embraces and kisses them, and sends them off with wagons, provisions, clothing, and gifts, including three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothing for Benjamin.

The brothers are terrified and unable to answer when Joseph reveals himself, and he tells them not to be grieved or angry with themselves for having sold him. After Joseph kisses them they talk with him, receive Pharaoh's commands and Joseph's gifts, and travel to Canaan, where they tell Jacob that Joseph is alive and ruler of Egypt.

Jacob, called Israel, is the father Joseph asks about and wants brought down to Egypt. When his sons tell him Joseph is alive, his heart faints and he does not believe them, but when he sees the wagons Joseph sent his spirit revives, and he says he will go see Joseph before he dies.

Pharaoh and his servants are pleased to hear that Joseph's brothers have come. He tells Joseph to have them bring their father and households in wagons, promising them the good and the fat of the land of Egypt, and says they need not worry about their belongings.

Joseph says God sent him ahead of his brothers to preserve life, to preserve a remnant for them, and to save them by a great deliverance. He says it was God, not the brothers, who sent him to Egypt and made him father to Pharaoh and ruler over the land.

Egypt is where Joseph rules as lord of all the land, and its people and Pharaoh's house hear his weeping. The famine, with five years remaining, continues there, and Pharaoh offers its best land and goods to Joseph's family, who are to settle in Goshen, and its wagons and good things are sent to Jacob.
Canaan is the land where Jacob lives and to which the brothers travel with Pharaoh's wagons and Joseph's provisions. There they tell Jacob that Joseph is alive, and Jacob decides to go see him.

l: Joseph's revelation to his brothers, Genesis, Chapter 45
s: Joseph, unable to restrain himself, sends everyone else out and says "I am Joseph!", leaving his brothers terrified and speechless until he asks them to come near. He reassures them that God, not they, sent him to Egypt to preserve life, after which he weeps, embraces and kisses them, and they talk with him.

Israel (Jacob) travels to Beersheba with all his possessions and offers sacrifices, and God speaks to him in a night vision, telling him not to fear going down to Egypt, where God will make him a great nation, go with him, and bring him back up, with Joseph closing his eyes. Jacob, his sons, their wives, little ones, and livestock travel to Egypt in wagons Pharaoh had sent. The chapter lists the names of the descendants who came with him through Leah, Zilpah, Rachel, and Bilhah, totaling seventy souls in the house of Jacob in Egypt. Jacob sends Judah ahead to Goshen, and Joseph goes to meet his father there, weeping on his neck, after which Israel says he is ready to die. Joseph instructs his brothers to tell Pharaoh they are keepers of livestock so they may settle in Goshen, since every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.

Jacob (Israel) goes to Beersheba, offers sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac, and receives God's promise in a night vision to go down to Egypt. He travels there with all his offspring, sends Judah ahead to Goshen, and weeps with Joseph on meeting him, saying he can now die since he has seen Joseph alive.

God speaks to Israel in visions of the night, calling 'Jacob, Jacob!' and identifying himself as the God of his father. He promises to make Jacob a great nation in Egypt, to go down with him and bring him up again, and that Joseph's hand will close his eyes.

Joseph is said to have had Manasseh and Ephraim born to him in Egypt by Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. He prepares his chariot and goes to Goshen to meet his father, falling on his neck and weeping, then instructs his brothers on what to tell Pharaoh so they can dwell in Goshen.
Pharaoh had sent wagons to carry Jacob and his family to Egypt. Joseph plans to tell him that his brothers and father's house have come, and expects Pharaoh to summon them and ask their occupation.

Egypt is the destination God tells Jacob not to fear, where he will be made a great nation. Jacob's household of seventy souls comes there, and it is noted that every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.

Judah is sent ahead to show the way to Goshen, and Jacob's party arrives in the land of Goshen. Joseph meets his father there and plans for the family to dwell there, apart from the Egyptians who despise shepherds.

l: Jacob's family (house of Jacob), Genesis, Chapter 46
s: The chapter lists the descendants of Jacob through Leah (thirty-three), Zilpah (sixteen), Rachel (fourteen), and Bilhah (seven), including sons, grandsons, and daughters. Those who came into Egypt were sixty-six direct offspring, and with Joseph's two sons born in Egypt, the house of Jacob numbered seventy.

l: journey of Jacob's family to Egypt, Genesis, Chapter 46
s: Jacob's sons carry him, the little ones, and the wives in Pharaoh's wagons from Beersheba, bringing their livestock and goods gained in Canaan. All his offspring go with him into Egypt, and they come into the land of Goshen.

l: reunion of Jacob and Joseph, Genesis, Chapter 46
s: Joseph goes up in his chariot to Goshen, presents himself to Israel, falls on his neck, and weeps a good while. Israel says he may now die, having seen that Joseph is still alive.

Joseph presents his father Jacob and five of his brothers to Pharaoh, who grants the family the land of Goshen (also called the land of Rameses) and offers to put capable brothers in charge of his livestock. Jacob tells Pharaoh his life has been 130 years of few and evil days, and blesses him. As the severe famine continues, Joseph collects all the Egyptians' and Canaanites' money, then their livestock, and finally their land and persons in exchange for bread and seed, making all Egypt's land Pharaoh's except the priests' land and setting a fifth of the harvest as Pharaoh's share. Israel's family prospers in Goshen, and after Jacob has lived 17 years in Egypt and reached age 147, he makes Joseph swear to carry him out of Egypt and bury him with his fathers.

Joseph reports his family's arrival to Pharaoh, presents five of his brothers, and settles his father and brothers in the best of the land, providing them with bread. He collects all the money, then the livestock, then the land of the Egyptians for Pharaoh, moves the people to the cities, and sets a statute that Pharaoh receives a fifth of the harvest. At the end he promises and swears to Jacob that he will bury him in his fathers' burying place rather than in Egypt.

Pharaoh questions Joseph's brothers about their occupation, grants them the land of Goshen, and tells Joseph to put any able men among them in charge of his livestock. He asks Jacob his age and is blessed by him twice. Through Joseph's actions he comes to own all the land of Egypt except the priests' land, and is entitled to a fifth of the harvests.

Jacob is brought before Pharaoh, blesses him, and says his 130 years of pilgrimage have been few and evil, not reaching the days of his fathers. He lives 17 years in Egypt and dies-to-be at 147, and, called Israel, he makes Joseph swear to carry him out of Egypt and bury him in his fathers' burying place, then bows himself on the bed's head.

Five of Joseph's brothers are presented to Pharaoh and say they are shepherds, as their fathers were, who have come to live as foreigners because of the famine in Canaan. Pharaoh gives them Goshen, and they, with their father's household, are provided with bread by Joseph.

When their money fails, the Egyptians give Joseph their livestock for bread, and in the second year offer their bodies and lands to Pharaoh in exchange for food and seed. They are moved to the cities, receive seed, agree to give a fifth of the harvest to Pharaoh, and say Joseph has saved their lives and that they will be Pharaoh's servants.

The land of Egypt, along with Canaan, faints from lack of bread during the famine. All its land except the priests' land becomes Pharaoh's, and Joseph's statute that Pharaoh receives a fifth remains in force to the time of writing. Part of it, Goshen or Rameses, is the best of the land given to Jacob's family, who become fruitful and multiply exceedingly there.

The famine is described as very severe in both Egypt and Canaan, leaving no bread in all the land and causing both lands to faint. It drives Jacob's family to Egypt and exhausts the people's money, then their livestock, and finally their land, leading to the Egyptians' sale of themselves and their fields.

Joseph buys all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh as each Egyptian sells his field because of the famine, with the exception of the priests' land, since the priests had a portion from Pharaoh. The people are moved to the cities and given seed, with a fifth of the harvests owed to Pharaoh and four parts kept for seed and food, a statute Joseph made.

As his death nears, Israel asks Joseph to place his hand under his thigh and deal kindly and truly by not burying him in Egypt but carrying him to his fathers' burying place. Joseph agrees, and when Israel asks him to swear, he swears.

Told that his father is sick, Joseph brings his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, to Jacob (also called Israel). Jacob recounts God Almighty's promise at Luz and declares that the two boys are his own, like Reuben and Simeon, and he recalls Rachel's death on the way to Ephrath. With dim eyes, Jacob kisses and embraces the boys, then blesses Joseph and the lads, crossing his hands so that his right hand rests on the younger Ephraim. Joseph objects because Manasseh is the firstborn, but Jacob refuses, saying Manasseh will be great while Ephraim will be greater. Jacob sets Ephraim before Manasseh, tells Joseph that God will bring them back to the land of their fathers, and gives Joseph one portion above his brothers.

Joseph is told his father is sick and brings his sons Manasseh and Ephraim to him, then bows with his face to the earth. He positions the boys so Manasseh is at Jacob's right hand, and is displeased when Jacob lays his right hand on Ephraim, trying to move it. Jacob refuses his objection, blesses him, and gives him one portion above his brothers.

Jacob, also called Israel, strengthens himself and sits up on the bed to receive Joseph, and recounts God Almighty's promise at Luz and Rachel's burial near Ephrath. Though his eyes are dim, he claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his own, blesses them with crossed hands, and refuses Joseph's attempt to correct him. He announces that he is dying, that God will be with Joseph, and that he has given Joseph a portion taken from the Amorite with his sword and bow.

Manasseh is Joseph's firstborn son, born in Egypt, and Jacob declares him to be his own like Reuben and Simeon. Jacob lays his left hand on Manasseh's head, and says he will become a people and be great, though his younger brother will be greater.

Ephraim is Joseph's younger son, born in Egypt, whom Jacob claims as his own like Reuben and Simeon. Jacob lays his right hand on Ephraim's head, saying his offspring will become a multitude of nations and that he will be greater than Manasseh, and sets him before Manasseh.

God Almighty is recalled as having appeared to Jacob at Luz in Canaan, blessing him and promising fruitfulness, a company of peoples, and the land as an everlasting possession. Jacob describes him as the God before whom Abraham and Isaac walked, who has fed him all his life, and whose angel redeemed him from all evil. Jacob says God will be with Joseph and bring them again to the land of their fathers.

l: Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh, Genesis, Chapter 48
s: Jacob blesses Joseph and the two lads, invoking the God of Abraham and Isaac and asking that his name and theirs be named on the boys and that they grow into a multitude. He deliberately crosses his hands, putting his right on the younger Ephraim, and over Joseph's protest says Ephraim will be the greater. He declares that Israel will bless in their name, saying 'God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh,' and sets Ephraim before Manasseh.

Jacob summons his sons to tell them what will happen to them in the days to come, and speaks a blessing or pronouncement over each of the twelve tribes. He rebukes Reuben for defiling his bed, condemns the violence of Simeon and Levi and says he will scatter them, and exalts Judah as a lion's cub whose scepter will not depart. He then characterizes Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Joseph, and Benjamin, giving Joseph the fullest blessing. Jacob charges his sons to bury him with his fathers in the cave of Machpelah in the field Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite. After finishing his charge, he gathers his feet into the bed, breathes his last, and is gathered to his people.

Jacob, also called Israel, gathers his sons and speaks to each of them about what will happen in the days to come. He then charges them to bury him in the cave of Machpelah, and after finishing, he gathers his feet into the bed, breathes his last, and is gathered to his people.

The sons of Jacob are summoned to assemble and hear their father's words about their future. Each receives his own blessing, and they are then instructed to bury Jacob with his fathers in the cave of Machpelah.

Jacob calls Reuben his firstborn, his might and the beginning of his strength, excelling in dignity and power. Because Reuben went up to his father's bed and defiled it, Jacob says he is boiling over like water and will not excel.

Jacob names Simeon as a brother of Levi, with swords that are weapons of violence. He says they killed men in anger and hamstrung cattle in self-will, curses their fierce anger, and says he will divide and scatter them in Israel.

Jacob names Levi as a brother of Simeon, with swords that are weapons of violence. He says they killed men in anger and hamstrung cattle in self-will, curses their cruel wrath, and says he will divide and scatter them in Israel.

Jacob says Judah's brothers will praise him, his hand will be on the neck of his enemies, and his father's sons will bow before him. He is called a lion's cub, and the scepter will not depart from him until he comes to whom it belongs, to whom the obedience of the peoples will be given.

Jacob calls Joseph a fruitful vine by a spring whose branches run over the wall. Though archers grieved and persecuted him, his bow remained strong by the Mighty One of Jacob, and the blessings of his father will rest on the head of him who is separated from his brothers.

l: twelve tribes of Israel, Genesis, Chapter 49
s: The twelve tribes of Israel are identified as the sons Jacob has just addressed, each described in his own pronouncement. The text says Jacob blessed everyone according to his own blessing.

Jacob names the cave in the field of Machpelah, before Mamre in the land of Canaan, as his desired burial place. Abraham bought it with the field from Ephron the Hittite, and Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah are buried there.

Jacob's blessings are individual pronouncements over each son, some of rebuke and some of praise or promise, concerning what will happen to them. The narrator says he blessed everyone according to his own blessing, and Joseph's blessing is said to prevail above the blessings of Jacob's ancestors.

Jacob instructs his sons to bury him with his fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite at Machpelah, bought by Abraham as a burial place. He gives this charge because he is about to be gathered to his people, and when he finishes charging them he dies.

Joseph mourns his father Israel and has him embalmed, then obtains Pharaoh's permission to bury him in Canaan as Israel had made him swear. A great Egyptian company goes up with Joseph and his brothers, mourns at the threshold floor of Atad (named Abel Mizraim), and Israel's sons bury him in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre. After the return to Egypt, Joseph's brothers fear he will repay them and send a message citing their father's request for forgiveness; Joseph weeps, tells them not to be afraid, says God meant their act for good, and promises to provide for them. Joseph lives to one hundred ten, sees Ephraim's children to the third generation, makes the children of Israel swear to carry his bones up when God visits them, and dies and is embalmed in a coffin in Egypt.

Joseph weeps over his father, has him embalmed, secures Pharaoh's permission, and leads the funeral party to Canaan to bury him. When his brothers fear revenge, he reassures them, saying he is not in God's place and that God meant their evil for good, and he promises to provide for them. He lives to one hundred ten, sees Ephraim's children to the third generation, makes Israel's children swear to carry up his bones, and is embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt.

Israel is embalmed over forty days by Joseph's physicians, and the Egyptians weep for him seventy days. His earlier oath-bound wish to be buried in his own grave in Canaan is carried out by his sons at the cave of Machpelah. His brothers also claim that before he died he commanded that Joseph be asked to forgive them.
Pharaoh receives Joseph's request through his staff and tells Joseph to go up and bury his father just as he swore. His servants, the elders of his house and the elders of Egypt go up with Joseph.

Joseph's brothers go up with him to bury their father and return to Egypt. Fearing Joseph will hate them and pay them back for the evil they did, they send word citing their father's command to forgive, then fall before him and call themselves his servants. Joseph comforts them and speaks kindly to them, and later he tells them God will visit them and bring them up to the promised land.

God is presented by Joseph as the one who meant the brothers' evil for good, to save many people alive. Joseph also says God will surely visit the Israelites and bring them out of Egypt to the land he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Israel's burial takes place after a procession of chariots, horsemen, Egyptian elders and Joseph's family, a very great company. They lament seven days at the threshing floor of Atad beyond the Jordan, which the Canaanites then name Abel Mizraim. His sons bury him in the cave of the field of Machpelah near Mamre, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site.

The LORD calls to Moses from the Tent of Meeting and instructs him to tell the children of Israel how to offer offerings of livestock. Leviticus 1 gives procedures for the burnt offering in three forms: a male without defect from the herd, a male without defect from the flock (sheep or goats), and birds (turtledoves or young pigeons). The offerer brings the animal, lays a hand on its head for atonement, and kills it, while Aaron's sons, the priests, handle the blood and burn the offering on the altar. Each offering is described as an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to the LORD.

The LORD calls to Moses and speaks to him from the Tent of Meeting, giving instructions for offerings. He declares that burnt offerings made by fire, whether of herd, flock, or birds, are a pleasant aroma to him, and that the offerer is accepted before him.
Moses is called by the LORD from the Tent of Meeting and is told to speak to the children of Israel. He is the one who relays the instructions about offerings.

l: children of Israel, Leviticus, Leviticus / Chapter 1
s: The children of Israel are the audience Moses is told to address. They learn that anyone among them who offers an offering to the LORD must give livestock from the herd or the flock.

Aaron's sons, the priests, present and sprinkle the blood around on the altar, put fire on the altar, lay wood in order, and arrange the pieces, head, and fat on the wood. The priest burns the whole offering on the altar, and for birds he wrings off the head, drains the blood on the altar's side, and burns the bird.

l: Tent of Meeting, Leviticus, Leviticus / Chapter 1
s: The Tent of Meeting is the place from which the LORD speaks to Moses. Its door is the place where the offerer brings a herd animal for the burnt offering, and the altar stands at its door.

The altar stands at the door of the Tent of Meeting. Blood is sprinkled around on it, fire and wood are laid on it, and the burnt offerings are burned on it. A flock animal is killed on its north side, and the crop and feathers of a bird are cast beside it on the east part, in the place of the ashes.

The burnt offering may come from the herd, the flock, or birds, and an animal must be a male without defect. It is killed, cut into pieces, with the innards and legs washed, and burned whole on the altar as an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to the LORD. A bird is torn by its wings but not divided apart.

l: offerer (anyone of you), Leviticus, Leviticus / Chapter 1
s: The offerer brings the offering of livestock to the door of the Tent of Meeting so that he may be accepted before the LORD. He lays his hand on the head of the burnt offering to make atonement, kills the animal, skins it, cuts it into pieces, and washes the innards and legs.

Chapter 2 gives instructions for presenting a meal offering to the LORD. The offering is made of fine flour with oil and frankincense, brought to Aaron's sons, the priests, who burn a handful as a memorial on the altar. The chapter covers forms baked in the oven, on a griddle, or in a pan, and the portion left over belongs to Aaron and his sons as a most holy part. Yeast and honey are forbidden in offerings burned for the LORD, salt of the covenant must always be included, and a first fruits offering uses fresh heads of grain parched with fire and crushed, with oil and frankincense.

The meal offering is to be made of fine flour with oil and frankincense, and may be baked in the oven, made on a griddle, or made in a pan. It must contain no yeast or honey, must be seasoned with salt, and a memorial portion is burned on the altar while the remainder goes to Aaron and his sons. A first fruits version uses fresh heads of grain parched with fire and crushed, with oil and frankincense.

The LORD is the one to whom the meal offering is presented, and the burned memorial is an offering made by fire of a pleasant aroma to him. He forbids yeast and honey from being burned as an offering and requires the salt of the covenant of God in every offering.

Aaron's sons are the priests to whom the meal offering is brought; the priest takes a handful and burns the memorial on the altar. What is left of the meal offering belongs to Aaron and his sons as a most holy part of the offerings of the LORD made by fire.
Salt must season every meal offering, and it is called the salt of the covenant of God, which must not be lacking. The text states that salt is to be offered with all offerings.

Leviticus 3 gives the rules for the sacrifice of peace offerings, which a person may bring from the herd, the flock (a lamb), or as a goat. For each animal the offerer must present it without defect before the LORD, lay his hand on its head, and kill it at the Tent of Meeting, while Aaron's sons, the priests, sprinkle the blood around on the altar. The fat covering the innards, the two kidneys with the fat on them, and the cover on the liver (plus the entire tail fat for a lamb) are taken away and burned on the altar as an offering made by fire, a pleasant aroma to the LORD. The chapter ends by declaring a perpetual statute for all generations and dwellings that the people shall eat neither fat nor blood.
The LORD receives the sacrifice of peace offerings, which is presented before him. The burned fat is an offering made by fire of a pleasant aroma to him, and all the fat is declared to be his.

l: sacrifice of peace offerings, Leviticus, Chapter 3
s: The sacrifice of peace offerings may be brought from the herd, the flock, or as a goat, male or female, and must be without defect. Its procedure involves laying a hand on the head, killing at the Tent of Meeting, sprinkling the blood on the altar, and burning the fat on the altar as food of the offering made by fire.
Aaron's sons, the priests, sprinkle the blood of each offering around on the altar. They also burn the removed fat on the altar, on the burnt offering that lies on the wood on the fire.

l: offerer (the person bringing the offering), Leviticus, Chapter 3
s: The offerer brings an animal without defect before the LORD, lays his hand on its head, and kills it at the Tent of Meeting. He also takes away the specified fat, kidneys, and liver cover as the offering made by fire.

l: herd animal (offering from the herd), Leviticus, Chapter 3
s: A herd animal, male or female, may be offered as a peace offering if it is without defect. It is killed at the door of the Tent of Meeting after the offerer lays a hand on its head, and its fat, kidneys, and liver cover are burned on the altar.

l: lamb (offering from the flock), Leviticus, Chapter 3
s: A lamb from the flock, male or female and without defect, may be offered as a peace offering before the LORD. In addition to the innard fat, kidneys, and liver cover, its entire tail fat is taken away close to the backbone and burned as the food of the offering made by fire.

A goat may be offered as a peace offering before the LORD, with a hand laid on its head and the kill made before the Tent of Meeting. Its innard fat, two kidneys with their fat, and liver cover are burned by the priest on the altar for a pleasant aroma.
The altar is where the blood of the offerings is sprinkled around by Aaron's sons. The fat portions are burned on it, on the burnt offering on the wood on the fire.

The fat covering the innards, the fat on the kidneys by the loins, the liver cover, and for a lamb the tail fat are taken away and burned on the altar. The text states that all the fat is the LORD's, and the people are forbidden to eat it.
The blood of each peace offering is sprinkled around on the altar by Aaron's sons. The people are forbidden to eat blood as part of a perpetual statute.

l: perpetual statute against eating fat and blood, Leviticus, Chapter 3
s: The chapter closes with a perpetual statute for all generations and in all dwellings. It commands that the people shall eat neither fat nor blood.

The LORD instructs Moses to tell the children of Israel how to handle unintentional sins against His commands. Different offenders bring different sin offerings: the anointed priest brings a young bull, the whole congregation brings a young bull with the elders laying hands on it, a ruler brings a male goat, and a common person brings a female goat or lamb. In each case the offerer lays a hand on the animal, it is killed before the LORD, and the priest applies its blood to the altar and burns the fat. The bull's remains for the priest and the congregation are burned outside the camp. The priest makes atonement, and the offender is forgiven.

The LORD speaks to Moses and gives the instructions for sin offerings for unintentional sins. He specifies the offering required from each class of offender and promises forgiveness after atonement. The fat burned on the altar is described as a pleasant aroma to Him.

l: whole congregation of Israel, Leviticus, Chapter 4
s: If the whole congregation sins and the matter is hidden from the assembly, then once the sin is known the assembly must offer a young bull as a sin offering. The elders lay their hands on its head, and after the prescribed rites the priest makes atonement and they are forgiven.

If the anointed priest sins so as to bring guilt on the people, he offers a young bull without defect as a sin offering. He also performs the blood rites: he sprinkles blood seven times before the veil, puts blood on the horns of the incense altar, and pours out the rest at the base of the altar of burnt offering. In the congregation's case he carries out the same rites, and in the cases of the ruler and the common person he applies the blood and makes atonement.

When a ruler unwittingly sins and the sin is made known to him, he must bring a male goat without defect as his offering. He lays his hand on it and it is killed, and after the priest's rites he is forgiven.

When one of the common people unwittingly sins and it is made known to him, he brings a female goat without defect. He may alternatively bring a female lamb without defect. After the priest makes atonement, he is forgiven.

The sin offering is the prescribed sacrifice for unintentional sins, with the animal varying by the status of the offender.
