The offerer lays a hand on its head, it is killed, its blood is applied to the altar, and its fat is burned, like the fat of the peace offerings. The text itself calls the goat "a sin offering" and the congregation's bull "the sin offering for the assembly."

The chapter addresses sins done unintentionally or unwittingly, in any of the things the LORD has commanded not to be done. It covers the anointed priest, the whole congregation, a ruler, and the common people. The offering is required when the sin becomes known, and it makes the offender guilty until atonement is made.

After the sin offering is made, the priest makes atonement for the offender or group. The text states that they "shall be forgiven" or "will be forgiven." This is stated for the congregation, the ruler, the common person, and the one who brings a lamb.

A young bull without defect is the sin offering for the anointed priest and for the whole congregation. It is killed at the door of the Tent of Meeting before the LORD. Its fat is burned on the altar, and the rest of it (skin, meat, head, legs, innards, dung) is carried outside the camp to a clean place where ashes are poured out and burned on wood.

The ruler's sin offering is a male goat without defect. He lays his hand on its head and kills it where the burnt offering is killed before the LORD. The priest puts some of its blood on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, pours out the rest at the base, and burns all its fat on the altar.

The Tent of Meeting is where the bull for the priest and for the congregation is brought, at its door, before the LORD. The priest brings the blood inside, sprinkles it before the veil of the sanctuary, and puts some on the horns of the altar of sweet incense. The altar of burnt offering stands at its door.

The altar of burnt offering is at the door of the Tent of Meeting. The rest of the blood of each sin offering is poured out at its base, and the blood of the ruler's and common person's offerings is put on its horns. The fat of the sin offerings is burned on it.

Blood is central to the sin offering rites. For the priest and the congregation it is sprinkled seven times before the veil and put on the horns of the altar of sweet incense. For the ruler and the common person it is put with the priest's finger on the horns of the altar of burnt offering. In all cases the rest is poured out at the base of the altar of burnt offering.

Chapter 5 lists situations in which a person incurs guilt: failing to testify after a public adjuration, touching unclean animal carcasses or human uncleanness unknowingly, and swearing rashly. The guilty person must confess and bring an offering to the LORD, with the priest making atonement. The offering scales to means: a female lamb or goat, then two turtledoves or young pigeons, then a tenth of an ephah of fine flour without oil or frankincense. The LORD then tells Moses that unwitting trespass against holy things requires a ram without defect, restitution, and an added fifth given to the priest. Unwitting violation of any of the LORD's commands still brings guilt and requires a ram as a trespass offering, after which the person is forgiven.

The LORD receives the sin and trespass offerings brought by guilty persons. He speaks to Moses, setting out a ram trespass offering with restitution for unwitting trespass against his holy things. He declares that a person who unknowingly breaks his commands is still guilty before him.

The priest makes atonement for the guilty person in each case, after which the person is forgiven. He offers the birds, wringing off the head of the sin offering without severing it and handling the blood at the altar. He burns a handful of the flour as a memorial portion, keeps the remainder as a meal offering, and receives the restitution plus a fifth.

l: sinner (the person who sins), Leviticus, Chapter 5
s: The person who sins becomes guilty by failing to testify, touching uncleanness unknowingly, swearing rashly, or trespassing unwittingly against holy things or commands. He must confess, bring an offering suited to his means, and make restitution where holy things are involved. Through the priest's atonement he is forgiven.

The sin offering is a female lamb or goat, or if the person is poor, one of two turtledoves or young pigeons, or if poorer still, a tenth of an ephah of fine flour. The flour has no oil or frankincense. The bird's blood is sprinkled on the altar's side and drained at its base.

The term covers the offering the guilty person brings to the LORD for his sin, including the lamb, goat, or birds. For unwitting trespass it is specifically a ram without defect valued in silver by the sanctuary shekel. It is declared that the one who brings it is certainly guilty before the LORD.

Atonement is made by the priest for the guilty person concerning his sin, each time after the required offering. It results in the person being forgiven. It is made with the ram in the cases of trespass against holy things and unwitting sin.

A ram without defect from the flock is the required trespass offering for unwitting trespass against the LORD's holy things and for unknowingly breaking his commands. It is valued in silver by the shekel of the sanctuary. The priest makes atonement with it, and the person is forgiven.

Unwitting sin, whether trespass against the LORD's holy things or doing what he commanded not to be done, still leaves the person guilty to bear his iniquity even though he did not know it. It requires a ram as a trespass offering. For holy things, restitution plus a fifth is also required, and forgiveness follows.

In Leviticus 6, the LORD speaks to Moses about offenses against a neighbor, requiring the guilty person to restore what was taken plus a fifth and bring a ram as a trespass offering, through which the priest makes atonement. The LORD then instructs Moses to command Aaron and his sons on the law of the burnt offering, including the nightly burning on the altar, the priest's removal of ashes, and the perpetual altar fire. The chapter gives the law of the meal offering, of which Aaron's sons eat the remainder unleavened in a holy place, and the special meal offering for the anointed priest, which is wholly burned. Finally, it sets out the law of the sin offering, which is killed where the burnt offering is killed, eaten by the offering priest and the male priests in a holy place, with rules for handling blood-stained garments and cooking vessels, and with the exception that any sin offering whose blood is brought into the Tent of Meeting must be burned.

The LORD speaks to Moses four times in this unit, giving laws on trespass restitution, the burnt offering, the meal offering, and the sin offering. He receives the offerings as a pleasant aroma and assigns the priests their portion of the offerings made by fire.
Moses is the recipient of the LORD's instructions throughout the unit. He is told to speak to or command Aaron and his sons regarding the laws of the offerings.

Aaron and his sons are commanded to follow the laws of the burnt offering and sin offering, and they eat the remainder of the meal offering. Aaron's own offering, made on the day he is anointed, is one tenth of an ephah of fine flour, half in the morning and half in the evening.

The sons of Aaron offer the meal offering before the LORD at the altar and eat what remains of it unleavened in the court of the Tent of Meeting. Every male among them has a perpetual portion of the offerings made by fire, and whoever touches them becomes holy. The anointed priest from among his sons offers the wholly burned meal offering.

The priest makes atonement for the guilty person with the trespass offering and tends the altar by putting on linen garments, removing the ashes, burning wood each morning, and carrying the ashes outside the camp in other garments. He eats the sin offering he offers in a holy place, and every male among the priests may eat it. A priest's own meal offering must be wholly burned and not eaten.
